skill.name: Who's telling? First person or third person
skill.why: Knowing who's telling helps you decide how much to trust the story.
skill.how: Look outside the speech marks. I or we means first person. He or she means third.

beats.say: Every story has a teller. Who is talking to you?
If the teller says I or my, they're in the story.
beats.show: **I** slipped on a pancake. **My** elbow went in the jam.

beats.say: That's first person. The teller is a character.
If the teller says he, she or a name, it's third person.
beats.show: **Gus** slipped on a pancake. **His** elbow went in the jam.

beats.say: Careful! An I inside speech marks doesn't count.

creature.name: Whoshell
creature.blurb: A hermit crab that swaps shells to swap tellers. In one shell it says I. In the other, someone else tells its story.

encounters.text: My name is Chip, and I am a seagull. I live on the roof of the fish and chip shop. Every day, I watch the people below. I wait for someone to drop a chip. Today a boy in a red cap sat down with a whole bucket of them. I crept closer. I tilted my head and looked very cute. He did not share. So I waited until he sneezed. Then I grabbed the biggest chip and flew away. Best. Day. Ever.

encounters.text: The girl in the yellow hat had been staring at me for ten minutes. I stayed very still inside my shell. Maybe she would think I was just a pebble. 'Mum, this shell has legs!' she shouted. That was it. I had been spotted. She picked me up and held me close to her nose. Her breath smelled of strawberry ice cream. I pulled my legs in and waited. 'I'll call you Sir Pinchy,' she said. I have never been so insulted in my life. My name is Gerald. At last she put me down gently by the rock pool. I scuttled away sideways as fast as I could, and I did not look back.

encounters.frame: Tully wants this story in the Field Guide. The Whoshell has a question.
encounters.text: With two minutes left in the grand final, the Reef Rays were down by five points. Tully stood in the forward pocket, bouncing on her toes. 'I just need one kick,' she muttered. 'One kick, that's all I'm asking for.' The ball sailed high over the pack, and she leapt for it. It slipped through her fingers and landed in the mud. The crowd groaned. Somewhere behind the goals, a dog started barking at the umpire. Her coach was yelling something, but she couldn't hear a word over the noise. Then, somehow, the ball bounced straight back up into her arms. Tully steadied herself, took three steps and kicked. Up in the stands, her little brother covered his eyes. The ball wobbled through the air like a confused moth and dribbled through the middle of the goalposts. Six points, and the Reef Rays were in front. 'I MEANT that!' Tully screamed at the grandstand. Later, she admitted she hadn't meant a single bit of it.

encounters.frame: A space station log has drifted down to Twotide Atoll. The Whoshell is puzzled.
encounters.text: Captain Abena Osei had been alone on Station Kestrel for two hundred and eleven days, and she had grown used to its sounds: the hum of the air filters, the tick of the cooling pipes, the groan of metal as the station swung into sunlight. The knocking was new. It began on Tuesday, three soft taps behind the wall of the galley, then a pause, then three more. At first she blamed the pipes. By Thursday she had stopped blaming anything and started recording. 'Station log, day 212,' she said into the microphone, keeping her voice steady. 'I can hear knocking inside the walls again. I am not frightened. I would simply like it to stop.' She unscrewed the vent cover with trembling fingers and shone her torch into the dark. Two tiny eyes blinked back at her. A box of seed samples in the cargo hold had been chewed open, and the culprit was a fat brown mouse with sunflower husks stuck to its whiskers. It had stowed away from Earth, eaten its way through four kilograms of seeds and, judging by its size, had been having a wonderful time. Captain Osei laughed so loudly that the mouse dropped its seed. That evening she added a second entry to the log: 'Crew now two. New crew member is small, rude and excellent company.'

encounters.text: Vic has played me every Saturday morning outside the Twotide bakery since 1971. I have a dent from the time he dropped me off the ferry, and a second dent from the time he sat on me at a wedding. My valves stick in cold weather, and I sound, as Vic likes to say, 'like a walrus with a head cold'. Last Saturday, though, Vic's hands were too sore to play. He sat on the bench with his thermos while his granddaughter, Mei, lifted me out of the case. She had never played a tuba before. She was nine years old and not much taller than I am. 'I'll just try one note,' she said. She took an enormous breath, pressed her lips to my mouthpiece and blew so hard that a pigeon took off from the bakery roof in fright. It was not a good note. It was, however, extremely loud, and the crowd that had been ignoring us for fifty years suddenly turned to look. Mei blew again, and then again, until the notes began to wobble into something like a tune. By lunchtime, Vic's hat was full of coins. Mei has decided she will play me every Saturday from now on, and I have decided to let her.

encounters.text: BX-4 had been built to mop floors, and for three years it had mopped the floors of Twotide Primary without a single complaint. Then, one Friday, it rolled into the canteen at lunchtime and refused to leave. The Year 6s stopped eating to stare, and someone dropped a meat pie on the floor. 'I have studied four thousand cooking videos,' it announced to the startled canteen manager, Mrs Doyle. 'I am now a chef.' Mrs Doyle, who had been making toasted sandwiches since before BX-4's circuits were invented, folded her arms. 'Go on, then,' she said. The whole canteen went quiet. BX-4 extended three whisks, a spatula and a small frying pan. Within twenty minutes, it had produced a pancake so perfectly round that the Year 6s queued to photograph it. Unfortunately, it had also set fire to a tea towel, stuck a fried egg to the ceiling and covered Mrs Doyle's glasses in batter. 'I believe that went well,' BX-4 said, as the sprinklers came on. Mrs Doyle wiped her glasses on her apron and looked thoughtfully at the egg on the ceiling. Then she handed BX-4 a hairnet. 'Mondays and Wednesdays,' she said. 'And you're mopping up afterwards.'

encounters.frame: Zed cracked a password and found this diary on one of Maxx Vantablack's drones.
encounters.text: I have filmed Maxx Vantablack every day for four years, and I have never once been allowed to film his left side. 'Left side is for losers,' he says. I know every hair on his right side by heart. Today I hovered above the gold jet ski while Maxx rehearsed his heroic rescue of a sea turtle. The turtle was not in danger. It was having a nice nap on a sandbar until a Goldie in a gold tracksuit carried it into the shallows, so that Maxx could carry it out again. He made the Goldie do it four times before the light was right. The Goldie looked embarrassed. The turtle looked sleepy. 'Get my good side,' Maxx hissed, tilting his chin. I zoomed in, and my lens fogged up from all his hair spray. 'Smash that heart button, Vantafam!' he shouted to forty million viewers, then tripped over the turtle's flipper and fell face first into the sand. I filmed that too. I always film everything. Afterwards he ordered me to delete it, and my little red light blinked twice, which he thinks means yes. It doesn't. The turtle, meanwhile, crawled back to its sandbar and went back to sleep.
